items.followUp: What is the difference between distance and displacement?

rubric.why: A scalar is distinguished by having magnitude only.
rubric.description: Defines a scalar quantity as having magnitude only.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a scalar has magnitude but no direction, or giving a correct scalar example.

rubric.why: A vector is distinguished by having both magnitude and direction.
rubric.description: Defines a vector quantity as having both magnitude and direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both properties, or giving a correct vector example with the defining properties.

modelAnswer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only and no direction, for example, mass.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction, for example, displacement.

items.followUp: Write the formula for centripetal acceleration and state what each symbol represents.

rubric.why: Centripetal force keeps an object moving in a circular path by acting towards the centre.
rubric.description: Defines centripetal force and gives its direction or role in circular motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it acts towards the centre of a circular path to keep an object moving in that path.

rubric.why: The mathematical form expresses the dependence of centripetal force on mass, speed and radius.
rubric.description: Writes a correct mathematical form of centripetal force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either standard formula, with symbols identified if required.

modelAnswer: Centripetal force is the force directed towards the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in that path.
Its mathematical form is F = mv²/r, where m is mass, v is speed and r is the radius of the circular path.

items.followUp: State the law of conservation of momentum and write its mathematical expression for a two-body collision.

rubric.why: The law states that the total momentum of an isolated system does not change.
rubric.description: States that total momentum remains constant in an isolated system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for clearly stating that the total momentum before and after interaction is the same.

rubric.why: The conservation statement applies when no resultant external force acts on the system.
rubric.description: Gives the condition for conservation or a correct two-body momentum equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the system is isolated/no external force acts, or writing the correct momentum equation.

modelAnswer: When no resultant external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
Therefore, total momentum before interaction equals total momentum after interaction.

items.followUp: What is inertia, and how does the mass of a body affect it?

rubric.why: Inertia is the property that opposes a change in motion.
rubric.description: Identifies inertia as resistance or opposition to a change in state.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that inertia resists a change in a body's state of rest or motion.

rubric.why: The state that inertia preserves is rest or uniform motion in a straight line.
rubric.description: Specifies the state of rest or uniform motion that a body tends to maintain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to rest and/or uniform motion.

modelAnswer: Inertia is the property of a body by which it resists a change in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line.

items.followUp: Two forces act on an object. What is the resultant force, and how can it be found?

rubric.why: A resultant force represents the combined effect of several forces as one force.
rubric.description: Defines resultant force as the single or net force equivalent to the forces acting together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the single force having the same effect as the combined forces.

rubric.why: The resultant is obtained by combining the forces, taking their directions into account.
rubric.description: Explains that the resultant is found by vector addition of the forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying vector addition or an equivalent correct method.

modelAnswer: The resultant force is the single force that produces the same effect as all the forces acting together on a body.
It is found by taking the vector sum of those forces.

items.followUp: Define the centre of mass and the centre of gravity of a body.

rubric.why: The centre of mass is the point at which the body's mass may be considered concentrated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as the point where the whole mass of the body may be considered concentrated.

rubric.why: The centre of gravity is the point through which the body's weight acts.
rubric.description: Defines the centre of gravity and distinguishes it from the centre of mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the whole weight of the body acts through this point.

modelAnswer: The centre of mass is the point at which the whole mass of a body may be considered concentrated.
The centre of gravity is the point through which the whole weight of a body acts.

items.followUp: A force of 10 N moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.

rubric.why: Work is done when a force causes displacement; it equals the product of force and displacement in the force's direction.
rubric.description: Defines work and/or gives its formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or the correct formula W = Fd for displacement in the direction of the force.

rubric.why: The SI unit of work is the joule, equivalent to a newton metre.
rubric.description: Names the SI unit of work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for joule (J) or N m.

modelAnswer: Work is done when a force causes displacement of a body; work equals the force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J), equivalent to the newton metre (N m).

items.followUp: Explain why heat flows from a hot body to a cold body, and name two sources of heat.

rubric.why: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, from higher to lower temperature.
rubric.description: Defines heat energy as energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that heat is transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of their temperature difference.

rubric.why: Examples of heat sources complete the requested response.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving at least two valid sources, such as the Sun, burning fuels, friction or electricity.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
Sources of heat include the Sun, burning fuels, friction and electricity.
